## Discussion

### Mechanistic insights into feeding dynamics

By decomposing the functional response into attack rate and handling time, this reanalysis reveals salinity-driven behavioral shifts that summary outcome metrics obscure. While @nandini2026 concluded that salinity did not have a significant effect on feeding behavior across the 10 to 30 g/L range, model in this study indicates a clear mechanistic divergence. Attack rates were credibly higher at 30 g/L compared to lower salinities, suggesting increased capture efficiency or higher baseline nematocyst functionality at higher osmotic concentrations. Conversely, handling time was credibly prolonged at 10 g/L compared to 20g/L, indicating a distinct physiological toll on the processing phase in lower-salinity environments.

Furthermore, the posterior contrasts support the directional prey preference observed in earlier studies (Nitokra > Apocyclops > Brachionus), but reframe it structurally. Rather than resting on a binary significance threshold, the model demonstrates that both copepods are processed with roughly half the handling time of the rotifer. This functional baseline provides a highly specific parameterized foundation for predicting the consumptive impact of C. caspia on plankton dynamics, replacing generalized counts with scalable biological rates.

### The inferential value of explicit causal frameworks

The divergence between these findings and those of a conventional two-way ANOVA highlights the inferential limits of Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) in ecological modeling. In the conventional approach, prey identity and salinity were modeled independently against raw counts and biomass. When those tests failed to reject the null for biomass, it licensed an assumption of "no effect."

By initiating the analysis with an explicit causal graph, the present workflow isolated the latent variables—$\alpha$ and $h$—that actually bridge the experimental design to the observed prey removal. Rather than asking if a summary outcome moved across a threshold, the Bayesian generative model yielded full posterior distributions for the mechanistic parameters themselves. This avoids treating a failure to falsify a strawman null as evidence of absence. Instead, it measures the magnitude and uncertainty of the biological drivers, proving that a non-significant biomass result can perfectly mask a highly credible shift in underlying attack and handling rates.

By formulating a single generative model focused strictly on the discrete biological event of prey capture, this workflow bypasses the garden of forking paths created by testing multiple algebraic transformations of the same data. Rather than asking if a summary outcome moved across an arbitrary threshold, the Bayesian generative model yields full posterior distributions for the mechanistic parameters themselves.

### Prior sensitivity and the limits of "the data will overwhelm the prior"

A common expectation in applied Bayesian work is that, with enough data, the posterior converges to what the likelihood alone would say regardless of the prior. That expectation is asymptotic: it holds as sample size grows large relative to the number of parameters being estimated, provided the prior does not rule out the data-favored value outright. Neither condition is automatically met in a design of this kind, and the salinity effect on attack rate in this reanalysis is a concrete illustration of why.

Four features of the present model work against the asymptotic expectation, none of them unusual for a controlled ecological experiment. First, the sample bearing on any one contrast is smaller than the nominal sample size suggests: 56 cell means inform roughly 33 free parameters jointly, and a specific pairwise contrast such as "20 g/L vs. 30 g/L" draws on only the subset of that data connected to those two levels. Second, the elicited priors are not vague. They were built from stated, literature-anchored fold-change claims (@sec-priors) specifically so that they would carry real information; a prior built to be informative should not be expected to vanish in the face of a likelihood that is itself only moderately informative at this sample size. Third, and specific to this model's structure, the zero-sum parameterization used for every main effect and interaction (@sec-stat-mdl) couples the levels of a factor rather than estimating them independently: a shift favored at one level must be compensated elsewhere in the same factor for the sum-to-zero constraint to hold, so tension between prior and likelihood at one level can surface as tension in the opposite direction at another, as it did here between 20 and 30 g/L. None of these conditions is exotic. They are close to the default case for a small controlled experiment estimating a richly structured effect, which is precisely the setting this paper's proposed workflow is meant for.

The practical resolution required direct checking. This direct checking relied on power-scaling sensitivity (psense) applied to the salinity effect on attack rate. This sensitivity metric flagged a genuine prior-data conflict at both 20 and 30 g/L. Left unexamined, this conflict risks triggering two opposite false alarms. The first alarm dismisses the salinity effect as a mere artifact of the prior. The second alarm declares the effect's direction entirely unknowable, a suspicion fueled by an earlier exploratory model that showed the reverse. Both alarms were silenced by systematically sweeping the prior's width. This sweep tested a range spanning from a tighter-than-elicited constraint out to an uninformative baseline. Across this entire baseline range, the sign of the 20–30 attack-rate contrast remained completely stable. Furthermore, the contrast actually grew in magnitude as the prior loosened. This growth proves the elicited prior is conservative compared to what the likelihood alone favors. Consequently, while the coefficient-level conflict is mathematically real, it does not alter the paper's interpretable, derived conclusions.

The general lesson is not that priors are dangerous or that Bayesian estimation is fragile; it is that "the data will sort it out" is an assumption, not a property that can be taken for granted in a small, multi-parameter design, and that the check is inexpensive relative to the alternative of either an unexamined false confidence or an unexamined false alarm. This is offered as a second, narrower illustration alongside the paper's central one: just as @nandini2026's own analysis benefited from an inferential layer that reports uncertainty rather than a threshold decision, the model built here benefits from treating its own prior choices as a further hypothesis to be checked against the data, rather than as a settled input. The reconciliation was extended to both pairwise salinity contrasts on attack rate (20 g/L vs. 30 g/L and 10 g/L vs. 30 g/L), which tracked one another closely across the swept range — a coherence check consistent with 10 and 20 g/L being themselves indistinguishable.

The prey$\times$salinity interaction cells that the same power-scaling check flagged received the equivalent sweep as well, on a derived quantity asking whether the 20–30 g/L attack-rate gap differs by prey (Nitokra vs. Apocyclops; Brachionus vs. Apocyclops; reported on the primary fit in @sec-attack-rate), and the outcome there differed in kind rather than degree. The Nitokra-vs-Apocyclops contrast is a stable non-finding: its HDI includes zero at every swept interaction-prior width, from tighter than elicited through markedly looser. The Brachionus-vs-Apocyclops contrast is directionally consistent — negative throughout — but its HDI excludes zero only at the loosest width tested (0.70), well past the elicited value (0.35), and includes zero at that elicited value itself. This is the reverse of the salinity main effect's pattern: there, widening the prior strengthened an interval that already excluded zero; here, widening the prior is what produces exclusion in the first place, so the apparent finding depends on adopting a prior looser than the one actually built from background knowledge, not on a robustness margin around it. Accordingly, this paper does not report a confirmed prey-dependent salinity effect on attack rate. The interaction term is retained in the model because the causal graph motivates it structurally (@sec-stat-mdl), but its magnitude is not treated as an established result. The asymmetry between the two checks — the salinity main effect surviving, the interaction not — is itself the clearest illustration in this reanalysis that a sensitivity check is not a formality to be passed on the way to a predetermined conclusion: it returns whichever answer is actually there, and reporting follows that answer rather than the other way around.

## Conclusion and Future Directions
Replacing the default NHST framework with an explicit causal graph and a Bayesian generative model does more than simply swap one statistical test for another; it changes the nature of the questions being answered. By analyzing the C. caspia dataset through the mechanistic lens of attack rate and handling time, this reanalysis recovered clear, salinity-driven behavioral shifts that conventional summary testing obscured. Crucially, it did so while quantifying the biological magnitude of those effects and openly stress-testing its own prior assumptions. The result is a robust, parameter-level understanding of an invasive predator's functional response, free from the false certainties of threshold-based $p$-values and the "garden of forking paths" created by testing multiple algebraic data transformations.

The reluctance to adopt these methods in marine science is understandable given the historical dominance of ANOVA and the perceived complexity of Bayesian modeling. However, as demonstrated here, the modern Bayesian workflow is accessible, rigorous, and strictly enforces the alignment of statistical models with underlying biological theory.

This paper has detailed the proposed workflow in its simplest application: a controlled experiment. Because experimental design intervenes on the treatment variables—here, salinity and prey identity—the causal relationships are identified without the need for covariate adjustment. However, marine ecology and biological oceanography are overwhelmingly observational sciences. When variables are measured in the field rather than controlled in a laboratory, the risk of unmeasured confounding drastically alters the inferential landscape.

In observational settings, the causal graph ceases to be merely a helpful structural guide and becomes an absolute necessity. It is the only formal mechanism for explicitly stating assumptions about environmental mediators, isolating direct from indirect effects, and identifying which backdoor paths must be closed to license a causal claim. The second paper in this series will extend this exact graph-first Bayesian workflow to observational marine field data, demonstrating how to handle confounding and causal identification when the researcher can no longer rely on experimental intervention.
